claims.text: The restaurant openly states that gluten-free items are prepared in the same kitchen as foods containing gluten. They use separate cooking equipment, such as frying oil and pans, and clean equipment thoroughly before each preparation - but because the kitchen is shared, a risk of trace cross-contact remains and the restaurant does not claim suitability for celiac disease.

For gluten-free dishes the restaurant says it uses ingredients that do not contain wheat, barley, rye, or non-gluten-free oats, and that it checks manufacturers' publicly available ingredient lists for seasonings. This relies on manufacturer declarations rather than independent testing or certification.

Gluten-free needs must be communicated to staff before ordering; the restaurant states it cannot take responsibility for orders where no prior notification was given. If you are celiac, flag it clearly when you arrive.

The published gluten-free policy says wheat, barley and rye are excluded from gluten-free dishes and that seasoning ingredient lists are checked, which implies a wheat-free seasoning is used for those dishes - but the sources do not specifically name the soy sauce or confirm it is wheat-free. Since standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, confirm directly with staff which seasoning is used on your dish.

Vegan and vegetarian options are offered alongside meat dishes, but the kitchen is shared with wagyu and other animal products, so strict vegans should expect possible cross-contact and confirm preparation with staff.

Staff aim to accommodate allergies where possible and ask guests to inform them at the time of ordering. They note, however, that because the kitchen shares equipment, severe allergies may not be fully supported.

Halal handling is taken seriously: staff are trained in halal procedures, the menu uses carefully selected halal-certified wagyu, no alcohol is used in cooking, and an on-site prayer room with ablution facilities is provided.

This is a genuinely allergy- and diet-aware restaurant: it maintains a dedicated gluten-free commitment that uses separate frying oil and pans for gluten-free orders and cleans equipment before each preparation.

Halal, vegan, vegetarian and gluten-free options are all available on one menu, with multilingual staff and menus (English, Chinese, Korean), making it unusually accommodating for travelers with dietary restrictions.
No alcohol is used in the dishes, which the restaurant states as part of its halal and inclusive approach.

name: 菜食料理エッフェ / Vegan Restaurant F

claims.text: The kitchen is wheat-flour-free throughout, with one exception: an ancient-grain spelt pasta. Spelt is a wheat variety and contains gluten, so it is not safe for celiacs, and there is no documentation of separate cookware or surfaces to keep this pasta from contaminating other dishes. Celiac diners should confirm directly how the spelt pasta is handled and ask for it to be left out.

One reviewer noted that gluten-free accommodation is available, but the spelt pasta still contains gluten, so 'gluten-free' here should be confirmed dish by dish with staff rather than assumed for the whole menu.
This is a fully vegan kitchen with no meat, fish, dairy, eggs, or refined white sugar used anywhere, so the risk of animal-product cross-contact is structurally very low.

The restaurant states it cannot accommodate vegetable allergies or oriental-style vegan requests (such as excluding the five pungent vegetables), and that gluten-free needs should be arranged in advance. Staff communicate in Japanese, with English menus available.
Aside from a single spelt-pasta option, the entire kitchen is built without wheat flour, meat, fish, dairy, eggs, or refined sugar, which removes many common allergens from the table.
House-baked rice-flour bread is offered as a gluten-free alternative to wheat bread.
Gluten-free meals can be arranged with advance notice.

This is a ramen shop where standard bowls use egg noodles and soy-sauce-based broths, prepared in a small shared kitchen run by two people. A gluten-free rice-noodle swap is offered, but no source documents separate pots, utensils, or surfaces, so cross-contact with wheat noodles and shared broth is likely. It should not be considered celiac-safe.
The signature ramen is a light soy-sauce (shoyu) broth; soy-sauce-based and miso broths in ramen typically contain wheat, so even the rice-noodle bowls may not be free of gluten in the soup itself.

The house style is a soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. There is no documentation that a wheat-free tamari is used, so celiac diners should assume the shoyu and miso broths contain gluten and confirm directly.

There is a dedicated separate menu for vegetarian and vegan dishes, and vegan bowls are made by swapping the egg noodles for rice noodles. Reviewers report a reliably plant-based experience, including three vegan ramens and fried mock 'soy meat,' though no source describes whether vegan and non-vegan items share cooking equipment.

The owner speaks English and is described as friendly and attentive; diners ask staff directly to swap egg noodles for the rice noodle option. No formal allergy protocol is documented, so describe your needs clearly when ordering.
Maintains a genuine separate vegan/vegetarian menu with three vegan ramens (miso, shoyu, curry) plus fried mock meat and veggie gyoza, which vegan diners praise highly.
A gluten-free rice-noodle option is available to replace the standard egg noodles on request.
English-speaking, hands-on owner in a tiny two-person shop makes it easy to ask questions about your order before you commit.

No source documents gluten-free preparation, a separate prep area, or cross-contamination controls. This is a cafe whose baked goods include wheat-flour items (for example whole-wheat cinnamon rolls and muffins), so flour is present and airborne in the kitchen. A celiac diner should not assume any item is gluten-free without confirming directly. The one item flagged as GF (a matcha cake) should be verified with staff before ordering.

No source specifies whether savory dishes use wheat-containing soy sauce or wheat-free tamari. As with most Japanese kitchens, assume standard soy sauce contains wheat unless staff confirm otherwise. Confirm directly if avoiding gluten.

This is a vegan-forward kitchen — reviewers describe vegan dishes as central to the menu and staff as genuinely vegan-aware, with plant-based mains, desserts, and soy milk widely available. No source raises vegan cross-contact concerns.

Staff speak English and there is an English menu, which makes asking about ingredients straightforward. However, no source documents a specific allergy-handling protocol, so allergic diners should describe their needs clearly and confirm individual dishes.
Strongly vegan-aware: plant-based dishes are central to the menu and reviewers consistently note knowledgeable, accommodating staff.
Soy milk and plant-based options are readily available for drinks and desserts.
English-speaking staff and an English menu make it easier to communicate dietary needs.

The doughnuts are made from 100% domestic Japanese wheat flour, so the standard doughnuts are NOT gluten-free and are not safe for celiac diners. The shop's own site describes the dough as made with domestic wheat, natural yeast, and rice koji.

A separate gluten-free menu is listed as available, but because wheat flour is the base of the regular doughnuts and is handled throughout the kitchen, cross-contamination is a real risk for celiac diners. No dedicated gluten-free prep area or fryer is documented — confirm directly with the shop before ordering.

All doughnut dough is made without eggs and without dairy, using natural yeast and rice koji, so the doughnuts are suitable for vegan diners. This is core to the shop's recipe rather than a special-request item.

The shop was started specifically to make egg-free, dairy-free doughnuts for a child with an egg allergy, so allergy-awareness is built into the business. Even so, no published details confirm how they handle gluten or other allergens in the kitchen — ask staff directly about your specific allergy.
Egg-free and dairy-free across the doughnut range, which removes two of the most common allergens and makes the doughnuts vegan-friendly by default.
Ingredients are carefully chosen and mostly domestic (Hokkaido wheat, the shop's own natural yeast, rice koji from a Kyoto sake brewery), reflecting an ingredient-conscious, allergy-aware approach.
A gluten-free menu and low-sugar options are listed alongside the vegan/vegetarian offerings, indicating they cater to multiple dietary needs.

This is a wheat-forward kitchen: the signature pizza uses a hand-stretched dough made from Hokkaido wheat, and the menu includes pasta and baked goods. Wheat flour is handled regularly, so even where a gluten-free dish exists, airborne flour and shared prep surfaces are a real cross-contact concern. No source documents how (or whether) gluten-free items are isolated from wheat handling. Celiac diners should not assume it is celiac-safe and must confirm preparation directly with staff.
A separate gluten-free menu is listed as available, but no details are published on dedicated equipment, separate prep areas, or cross-contamination controls.

No source specifies whether the soy sauce or seasonings used are wheat-free. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so savory dishes (e.g., the hayashi rice or teriyaki-style plate) should be assumed to contain wheat unless staff confirm a wheat-free soy sauce or tamari is used.
The entire kitchen is 100% plant-based with no meat or dairy on site, which substantially lowers the risk of animal-product cross-contact for vegan diners.

The restaurant's stated concept is 'food barrier-free' dining for people with allergies and varied dietary needs, and it advertises a gluten-free menu, suggesting allergy awareness. However, no concrete allergen-handling or cross-contamination protocols are published; confirm specifics with staff.
Fully vegan kitchen - all dishes are 100% plant-based with no meat or dairy, and an English menu is available.
A dedicated gluten-free menu is offered, and the restaurant explicitly markets itself to diners with allergies and dietary restrictions.
Ingredient sourcing emphasizes organic and pesticide-free Kyoto vegetables, which the restaurant highlights as a core priority.

No gluten-free menu or cross-contamination protocol is documented in available sources. The menu leans heavily on wheat: sandwiches, baguette, and pasta of the day are all core items, so the kitchen routinely handles wheat. This cafe should not be considered celiac-safe; a celiac diner would need to confirm directly with the staff before eating.

No information found on whether soy sauce or other seasonings used are wheat-free. As most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, anyone strictly avoiding gluten should ask the staff directly about seasonings.
The entire menu is fully vegan, so there is no animal-product cooking line to cross-contact with. This makes it a comfortable choice for vegan diners.
No specific reports on how staff handle allergy requests. Ordering is counter-service (order and pay first, then take a seat), so flag any allergy clearly at the counter when ordering.
Fully vegan kitchen, so every dish is plant-based with no risk of animal-product cross-contact.
Small, made-with-care menu that guests consistently praise; the owner is attentive and responds personally to guest feedback.

No documented gluten-free protocol or cross-contamination procedure was found. The raw vegan sweets are explicitly made without wheat, but the savory menu (porridge sets) includes grains and items like natto crackers, so a strict celiac diner should confirm wheat-free status and shared-surface handling dish by dish directly with staff.

The cafe makes its own miso and sauces and uses fermented ingredients, but no source specifies whether the seasonings (including any soy sauce/tamari) are wheat-free. Since most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, a celiac diner should ask which house seasonings are used on the porridge and savory sides.
The food and beverages are described as 100% vegan, with no eggs or dairy used in the kitchen, which lowers the risk of animal-product cross-contact in the food.
Note that the attached retail corner has been reported as vegetarian rather than strictly vegan, so check individual products if buying goods.
The kitchen is fully plant-based (no eggs, no dairy), which is reassuring for vegan diners.
The 御所の杜 raw vegan sweets are explicitly free of eggs, dairy, wheat and added sugar.
The menu lists gluten-free and sugar-free options, including the wheat-free raw desserts, giving GF diners documented choices to start a conversation from.
